subject: physics
title: Electron Diffraction and de Broglie
welcome_lead: Accelerate electrons through a voltage, then catch their wavelength on a crystal screen.
meta_desc: A-Level Quantum Phenomena adventure on electron diffraction and de Broglie matter waves.
final_note: Higher accelerating voltage → smaller λ → tighter diffraction rings.

concepts.def: More p, less λ, smaller rings.

walkthroughs.body_html: An electron through potential V gains eV of kinetic energy. So ½mv² = eV, giving p = √(2meV). The greater V, the greater p.
The momentum gives the de Broglie wavelength. At 5 kV, λ ≈ 17 pm — comparable to atomic spacings, perfect for diffraction off crystal lattices.
The polycrystalline target produces concentric rings. Ring radius gives diffraction angle, hence λ. Higher V tightens rings as λ shrinks.

mcqs.q: Increasing the accelerating voltage of electrons:
What determines the de Broglie wavelength of a particle?
options: Energy turns into mass according to E=mc^2 when waves cancel.
Its kinetic energy alone, with no dependence on mass.
Its momentum (lambda = h/p) — heavier or faster particles have shorter de Broglie wavelengths.

mcqs.q: When does an electron behave as a wave?
options: Energy turns into mass according to E=mc^2 when waves cancel.
Electrons are always waves and only look like particles at low energy.
Electrons are sometimes waves and sometimes particles depending on the temperature of the apparatus.
In experiments that probe wave properties (e.g. diffraction through a crystal); in particle-like experiments it behaves as a particle.

mcqs.q: When two waves interfere destructively, what happens to the energy?
options: Energy is destroyed at points of destructive interference.
Energy turns into mass according to E=mc^2 when waves cancel.
Energy is redistributed — there is constructive interference elsewhere, conserving total energy.
